title: The wretched man (Romans 7:14–25)
hookLine: the good I want, I don't do

lines: THE ALARM, THE SHOES, THE SNOOZE.
PAUL WRITES IN THE FIRST PERSON.
cards: The alarm is set for six. The running shoes are by the door. The plan was made with a clear head and good intentions.

Then six o'clock comes, and a hand reaches over and turns the alarm off. Or it's the sharp word someone swore they wouldn't say, out loud again. Wanting one thing and doing another is an old, ordinary human knot.
The surprise is finding it in Paul's letter to Rome, right after his big picture of new life. He stops arguing, and writes in the first person about a war inside him.

teach.h: THE GOOD THAT I WOULD I DO NOT.
teach.b: Here it is, in the King James Bible: "For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do." It doubles back on itself like the knot it describes. Paul says he agrees with God's law.
He delights in it. He knows it's good.
And still something in him pulls the other way, like a second law at war inside him. The knowing isn't the problem. The doing is.
Then the paragraph breaks open into a cry: "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" Wretched, talaiporos in Greek, means miserable, worn down by hardship.
It isn't a pose; it's a groan. And notice the question. Not how do I fix myself, but who shall deliver me?
He's looking outside himself. The answer comes in the very next breath: "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord."
Now a real puzzle Christians have argued over for a long time: who is this I?
Some readers, including Augustine in his later years and Martin Luther, hear the Christian life: even the baptized still feel this war inside, every day.
Others, among them early Greek teachers and scholars today, hear life under the law without the Spirit, the way things look before chapter eight.

teach.h: O WRETCHED MAN THAT I AM!
teach.b: The text doesn't settle it for us. Either way, Paul writes in the present tense, and he doesn't flinch. He doesn't hide the struggle or scold it.
He names it, and cries out for help.

how: Christians often turn to Romans 7 when talking honestly about habits and temptation, in confession, in recovery groups and in spiritual direction, where the struggle is named without shame.

o: hating yourself for being a bad person
worn down and miserable from long hardship
too lazy to keep doing what's right

games.q: what's inside the paragraph — tap the pairs.

s: Paul says his problem is not knowing what's good
he knows the law is good and delights in it. the doing is the problem.
all Christians agree on who the I in Romans 7 is
some hear the Christian's daily struggle; others hear life under the law without the Spirit.
Paul's cry is followed at once by thanks
"I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord."

games.q: you're Paul. you've admitted the good you want, you don't do. what comes next?
o: resolve to try much harder tomorrow.
cry out: who shall deliver me?
decide the law is too hard and drop it.
games.why: "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me?" he looks outside himself, and the next breath is thanks: "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord."

practice: Name one small, real thing you keep doing that you don't want to do, and instead of the usual lecture, speak to yourself the way you'd speak to a friend who told you the same thing: tired, honest, still trying.
Notice where the struggle sits in your body, and let your breath go there. If you pray, say Paul's own question, who shall deliver me, and just wait with it.

wordCard.voice: Talaiporos. Paul's Greek cry of wretchedness: worn down by the war between the good he wants and what he does.

orig.note: Greek: wretched, worn down, miserable from long hardship.

carryVoice: Your line: who shall deliver me? It's a cry for help, not a lecture. See you tomorrow.
